overview: Compsognathus longipes was one of the smallest non-avian dinosaurs, about the size of a turkey (0.65–1 m), from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen Limestone of Germany (~150 Ma). For over a century it held the record as the smallest known dinosaur, and the first specimen described was the most complete theropod known at the time — providing crucial evidence that dinosaurs were slender, active animals rather than lumbering reptiles.

The Solnhofen lagoon-margin environment where Compsognathus is found also preserves Archaeopteryx, and the similarity between the two — a small feathered theropod and a small non-feathered theropod of similar size — fuelled early debates about the origin of birds. Its stomach contents in both known specimens include small lizards, confirming it was a fast active predator.

fossilSites.name: Solnhofen Limestone
fossilSites.note: Late Jurassic (Tithonian) lagoonal deposits famous for exceptional preservation; yields Compsognathus alongside Archaeopteryx and a diverse marine fauna.

fossilSites.name: Canjuers Limestone
fossilSites.note: Late Jurassic lagoonal deposits with the larger French Compsognathus specimen.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: The first specimen was found in Bavaria around 1859 and described by Johann Andreas Wagner in 1861, who initially classified it as a lizard. Thomas Henry Huxley recognised its dinosaurian nature and compared it to Archaeopteryx in 1868, arguing that it demonstrated the close relationship between dinosaurs and birds. A second, larger specimen from France described in 1978 may represent a distinct species (C. corallestris or a female with different proportions).

articles.title: Stomach contents and diet
articles.body: Both known specimens preserve the remains of small lizards in the stomach region. The German specimen contains a nearly complete skeleton of Bavarisaurus — a small, fast lizard — implying that Compsognathus was an active pursuit predator capable of catching agile prey. Its two-fingered hand (some relatives have three) shows early reduction of the hand in some coelurosaur lineages.

articles.title: Size and significance
articles.body: Compsognathus was the smallest adult dinosaur known for over a century until the discovery of smaller species in the Cretaceous feathered dinosaur record from China. Its small size, fine bones and active lifestyle made it the archetypal "bird-like" non-avian dinosaur in Victorian science, and it features in Conan Doyle's The Lost World (1912) as the miniature dinosaurs encountered by the expedition.

fossilRecord.formations: Solnhofen Limestone, Bavaria, Germany; Canjuers Formation, France
fossilRecord.material: Two articulated skeletons with exceptional soft-tissue detail; one preserves stomach contents.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Jurassic shallow lagoon environments in what are now southern Germany and southern France.
fossilRecord.evidence: Stomach contents document its diet of small lizards; exquisite preservation confirms body outline and limb proportions.

record.description: Compsognathus longipes was a small coelurosaur from the Tithonian lagoonal limestones of Germany and France. Two nearly complete skeletons of different sizes document its slender bipedal body; C. corallestris is generally treated as the same species.
facts: The smaller German specimen contains lizard remains in its abdominal region, direct evidence of predation or scavenging.
The larger French specimen shows that the famously tiny German individual was not the maximum adult size.

review.ageReviewNote: The Solnhofen and Canjuers lagoonal deposits are Tithonian.

residualUncertainty: The ontogenetic stage of each specimen is debated.
No direct feather impressions are known for Compsognathus itself.

evidence.material: Two nearly complete skeletons, one with gut-region prey remains.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Two good skeletons support anatomy and small-prey feeding; growth stage, feathers and population size range remain uncertain.
uncertainties: The ontogenetic stage of each specimen is debated.
No direct feather impressions are known for Compsognathus itself.
